Who Transfers Safety? Identifying and Targeting Cross-Lingual Shared Safety Neurons

Identify shared safety neurons that connect high-resource and non-high-resource language behaviour.

Zhang Xianhui · Xie Chengyu · Zhu Linxia · Yang Yonghui · Zhao Weixiang · Cheng Zifeng · Wang Cong · Shen Fei · Chua Tat-Seng

February 1, 2026 ·ICML 2026 ·Read the paper ·PDF ·Code
1Why this matters 2How it works 3What the study finds 4What this means

The short version

The study identifies a small shared subset of safety neurons across languages and uses targeted training to improve multilingual defensive consistency.

SharedCross-lingual safety neurons
CausalActivation and suppression tests
TargetedSelected-neuron alignment

Why this matters

A model’s safety behaviour can differ sharply across languages. Understanding which internal components participate in that transfer can guide more focused alignment.

How it works

  1. Identify monolingual safety neurons and test their role through activation and suppression.
  2. Find the subset shared between high-resource and non-high-resource languages.
  3. Train the selected shared subset with a strategy accounting for language resources and model architecture.

What the study finds

Suppressing shared neurons causes concurrent safety drops in non-high-resource languages, while reinforcement improves cross-lingual consistency. Targeted fine-tuning reports stronger non-high-resource safety than the compared methods while maintaining general capabilities.

What this means

Multilingual alignment can be investigated at the level of shared mechanisms, with interventions testing whether the selected components influence behaviour across languages.
